title: Comparing Linear Mixed Models, Generalized Estimating Equations, and Generalized Linear Mixed Models Under Monotone Missing-at-Random Dropout in Longitudinal Clinical Trials: A Monte Carlo Simulation Study
content: Background: Longitudinal clinical trials are often affected by dropout, which can influence statistical inference if not handled appropriately. This simulation study examined three widely used approaches for analyzing repeated measurements under monotone missing-at-random dropout: linear mixed-effects models (LME), generalized estimating equations (GEE), and generalized linear mixed models (GLMM). Methods: A factorial Monte Carlo design generated longitudinal datasets defined by patient, visit, and treatment group. Simulations included a continuous and a binary outcome under two effect-size scenarios, three sample sizes (100, 200, 500), and four dropout rates (10% to 40%), with 1000 replications per design cell. Gaussian LME and GEE were fitted to the continuous outcome; logistic GLMM and GEE to the binary outcome. Results: All four methods produced small, stable bias across the full design, and RMSE decreased with larger samples. Coverage of the nominal 95% interval stayed close to target, from about 93% to 96%, while Type I error remained near nominal. Power declined with dropout but exceeded 99% at N=500. Both GEE models converged in every replication; logistic GLMM converged less consistently, between 96% and 99%. The clearest difference concerned standard errors: robust sandwich estimates agreed closely with empirical variability, whereas naive model-based estimates, particularly for Gaussian GEE, consistently underestimated it. Conclusion: Under monotone missing-at-random dropout, reliable GEE inference depended on the robust sandwich variance estimator rather than the naive alternative. Comparisons between GLMM and GEE were meaningful only when each method was evaluated against its own estimand, conditional for GLMM and marginal for GEE.
